[untitled BTM module] Circulating monocytes find their way into tissue by reading chemokine gradients, and the two receptors that anchor this group, CCR2 and CX3CR1, are the pair that defines the classical and non-classical monocyte subsets and governs their recruitment to inflamed vessel walls, injured tissue and the brain, where they become macrophages or microglia. Loss or blockade of this axis limits atherosclerotic plaque myeloid influx and blunts inflammatory infiltration, which is why it is a longstanding drug target.
enriched in myeloid cells and monocytes

[untitled BTM module] A mixed immune-expression module centred on mononuclear leukocyte identity and trafficking, combining chemokine receptors, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators. Monocyte and macrophage recruitment to inflamed tissue depends on CCR2 and CX3CR1, whose ligands direct patrolling and infiltrating cells to vessel walls and injured sites; loss of this axis blunts inflammatory monocyte egress from bone marrow and reshapes atherosclerotic and neuroinflammatory disease.

[untitled BTM module] These genes form a brake system on leukocyte activation, tuning how strongly lymphocytes and myeloid cells respond to antigen receptor, Toll-like and cytokine receptor engagement. Restraint of this kind sets thresholds for activation, prevents autoimmunity and chronic inflammation, and is also what tumours exploit to blunt T cell responses, making several members attractive immunotherapy targets.

[untitled BTM module] These genes outline the myeloid identity and activation program of monocytes and macrophages, the cells that patrol tissue for microbes and debris and set the tone of an inflammatory response. The transcription factor SPI1 (PU.1) specifies this lineage together with HHEX, while TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide and PTAFR responds to platelet-activating factor, coupling through the Src-family kinase LYN, the phospholipase PLCB2 and the ITAM-bearing adaptor TYROBP (DAP12) to calcium mobilization and cytoskeletal change; DOK2 acts as a brake on this kinase signaling.
